items.stem: Which term describes a large, well-established religious organisation with a hierarchy of professional clergy, claiming a monopoly of truth and often linked to the state?
items.answer: Church
items.markingKey: Church: a large, well-established religious organisation with a hierarchy of professional clergy, claiming a monopoly of truth and often linked to the state. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “religious pluralism”, and give one example.
items.answer: The existence of many different religious organisations in a society. Example: churches, mosques, temples and sects in one city.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the existence of many different religious organisations in a society); 1 mark for a relevant example such as churches, mosques, temples and sects in one city. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “cult” and “religious pluralism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Cult: a loose, individualistic religious group with no sharp boundaries, offering services such as healing or self-improvement (e.g. astrology groups or New Age therapies). Religious pluralism: the existence of many different religious organisations in a society (e.g. churches, mosques, temples and sects in one city).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A religious organisation in Seoul has millions of members across the country, a hierarchy of professional priests and its leader takes part in state ceremonies. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: religion is ideology that legitimates class inequality and offers false comfort to the oppressed (“the opium of the people”), creating false consciousness (Marx, Lenin).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A religious organisation in Cairo has millions of members across the country, a hierarchy of professional priests and its leader takes part in state ceremonies. Explain how a Weberian sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religious ideas can bring about social change; beliefs such as the Protestant ethic shaped economic behaviour, and religion can motivate social movements (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research membership of different types of religious organisation.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public; definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying membership of different types of religious organisation but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: People in Singapore attend weekend workshops on “energy healing”; there is no membership, and many also go to their usual place of worship. Compare how postmodernist and religious market sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: religion has become a matter of individual choice and consumption; people pick and mix beliefs in a spiritual supermarket (Lyon, Heelas). Religious market theory: religion is a market: when there is competition and choice, religious organisations meet people’s needs and religiosity stays strong (Stark and Bainbridge).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: The table shows official membership figures for types of religious organisation in one country. Table: membership in a country (thousands) | 1980 | 2020. Churches | 2988 | 2043. Denominations | 993 | 638. Sects and new religious movements | 69 | 115. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Denominations between 1980 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that sects are growing while churches decline.
items.answer: (a) (638 − 993) ÷ 993 × 100 = -35.8%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Sects and new religious movements; the figure fell for Churches, Denominations; Churches had the highest figure for 2020. Religious pluralism increases choice. Qualifications: Sects remain very small; membership figures may be unreliable; growth from a small base looks large; many people believe without belonging. The data also come from official statistics of 3 members in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (638 − 993) ÷ 993 × 100; 1 mark for -35.8% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Distinguish between “new religious movement (NRM)” and “world-accommodating movement”, using an example of each.
items.answer: New religious movement (NRM): a religious or spiritual group of recent origin, outside the mainstream religions (e.g. the Unification Church or Transcendental Meditation). items.stem: Samuel, a sociology student, is designing a project on the experiences of members of a world-rejecting movement. Evaluate the use of semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can adapt questions sensitively while still covering the key issues; a core set of questions allows some comparison between interviewees while follow-up questions add depth. Limitations: follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule; samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of members of a world-rejecting movement but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Study the following extract (Source A) from a report on research carried out in Lima. “A researcher studied a new religious movement in Jakarta for six years, attending workshops and interviewing members and ex-members. Of 1,000 people who attended an introductory workshop, 80 joined the movement and only 40 were still members two years later. Most members were young, middle-class graduates.” (a) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that people join new religious movements through free choice rather than brainwashing.
items.answer: (a) 1. Only 8% of those attending a workshop joined. 2. Half of those who joined had left within two years. (b) For: The source shows low recruitment and high drop-out, as Barker found with the Moonies. Against: Some movements use manipulative techniques; ex-members report pressure; one movement may not be typical; the researcher’s presence may have affected behaviour; middle-class members may still be relatively deprived (Wallis). Also consider how far a single study using case studies can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research who joins new religious movements.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying who joins new religious movements but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using participant observation to research why people join sects.
items.answer: Strengths: it can give access to groups that would never complete a questionnaire, such as deviant subcultures; it is flexible and can uncover issues the researcher had not anticipated. Limitations: studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise; it is time-consuming, costly and may put the researcher at risk. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why people join sects but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).

items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they are often cheap to obtain and produced without the researcher influencing them. items.answer: (a) 20 − 31 = -11 percentage points (General population compared with Sect members). items.stem: The table shows official membership figures for types of religious organisation in one country. Table: membership in a country (thousands) | 1980 | 2020. Churches | 2796 | 1468. Denominations | 1173 | 703. Sects and new religious movements | 75 | 106. By how many thousand members did the figure for Denominations change between 1980 and 2020?
items.answer: -470 thousand members
items.markingKey: 703 − 1173 = -470 thousand members. [1]

items.stem: A group of 60 people near Bogotá follow a leader who claims to receive messages from God; members live together, give up their possessions and avoid contact with outsiders. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: religion is ideology that legitimates class inequality and offers false comfort to the oppressed (“the opium of the people”), creating false consciousness (Marx, Lenin).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful official statistics are for studying membership of different types of religious organisation.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they cover very large numbers of people, often a whole population, so they are representative. Limitations: interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying membership of different types of religious organisation but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes an NRM, often breaking from a mainstream church, that neither accepts nor rejects the world but focuses on religious life?
items.answer: World-accommodating movement
items.markingKey: World-accommodating movement: an NRM, often breaking from a mainstream church, that neither accepts nor rejects the world but focuses on religious life. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “world-affirming movement”.
items.answer: An NRM that accepts the world and offers members ways to succeed and fulfil their potential within it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: an NRM that accepts the world and offers members ways to succeed and fulfil their potential within it. [1]

items.stem: Explain two differences between world-rejecting and world-affirming new religious movements.
items.answer: Attitude to society (hostile vs accepting); commitment (total vs part-time); lifestyle (communal and separate vs normal lives); purpose (salvation or social change vs personal success and fulfilment); recruitment (often young vs often middle-class adults).
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained difference. [4]

items.stem: Read Source A. “A researcher studied a new religious movement in Singapore for six years, attending workshops and interviewing members and ex-members. Of 1,000 people who attended an introductory workshop, 80 joined the movement and only 40 were still members two years later. Most members were young, middle-class graduates.” (a) Identify the main research method used in the study described in Source A. (b) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study.
items.answer: (a) Case studies. (b) 1. Only 8% of those attending a workshop joined. 2. Half of those who joined had left within two years.
items.markingKey: (a) Case studies. [1] (b) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2]

items.stem: A group that split from a mainstream church in Seoul focuses on lively worship and spiritual renewal, while members keep ordinary jobs. Using Wallis’s typology, which type of new religious movement is described?
items.answer: World-accommodating
items.markingKey: World-accommodating: neither accepts nor rejects the world; focuses on religious life. [1]

items.stem: Source A: “A researcher studied a new religious movement in Kuala Lumpur for six years, attending workshops and interviewing members and ex-members. Of 1,000 people who attended an introductory workshop, 80 joined the movement and only 40 were still members two years later. Most members were young, middle-class graduates.” Use Source A and your own knowledge to answer the questions. (a) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that people join new religious movements through free choice rather than brainwashing.
items.answer: (a) 1. Only 8% of those attending a workshop joined. 2. Half of those who joined had left within two years. (b) For: The source shows low recruitment and high drop-out, as Barker found with the Moonies. Against: Some movements use manipulative techniques; ex-members report pressure; one movement may not be typical; the researcher’s presence may have affected behaviour; middle-class members may still be relatively deprived (Wallis). Also consider how far a single study using case studies can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Colombo wants to research who joins new religious movements. Evaluate the use of covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided; it can give access to closed or deviant groups who would refuse an overt researcher. Limitations: it involves deception and lack of informed consent, which breaks ethical guidelines; the study cannot be repeated, so reliability is low. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying who joins new religious movements but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes feeling deprived compared with others, even if not poor?
items.answer: Relative deprivation
items.markingKey: Relative deprivation: feeling deprived compared with others, even if not poor. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Niebuhr argued sects usually last unchanged for many generations.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. He argued sects either die out or become denominations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Wilson argued that rapid social change and anomie encourage the growth of sects. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Wilson argued disruption of norms leads people to seek certainty in sects. Criticism: Some established sects survive for generations.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Weberian theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Kwame surveyed 600 sect members in Santiago and compared them with the general population. Table: percentage in each group | Sect members | General population. Unemployed or in low-paid work | 42% | 27%. Recently moved to the city | 31% | 14%. Have a university degree | 22% | 31%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Sect members and General population for Recently moved to the city (General population minus Sect members)?
items.answer: -17 percentage points
items.markingKey: 14 − 31 = -17 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Professionals in Lisbon pay to attend weekend retreats that combine yoga, life coaching and Buddhist meditation, saying they want to “find their true selves”. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: religion is ideology that legitimates class inequality and offers false comfort to the oppressed (“the opium of the people”), creating false consciousness (Marx, Lenin).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful unstructured interviews are for studying why people join sects.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; the interviewee can raise issues the researcher had not thought of, so the research is not limited by pre-set categories. Limitations: samples are small, so findings are difficult to generalise; they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why people join sects but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
